Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones
A specific texture associated with the event

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I have to be on guard all the time
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: For a 55-year-old female bank teller with combat trauma, 'Bicycle' as a trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger items imply interpersonal/loss and sensory trauma reminders, while bicycle is a highly specific cue with no support from threat, memory, or appraisal content and no clear combat linkage. This makes it clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'You can never know who will harm you' is too nonspecific relative to the rest of the profile. The threat items emphasize overt vigilance and reading faces/body language, and the appraisals also center betrayal and loss of meaning. This item implies diffuse interpersonal mistrust without a corresponding interpersonal memory or trigger pattern beyond betrayal, making the negative appraisal set less coherent with the otherwise combat/loss-focused formulation.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise organized around combat-linked threat, sensory triggers, and disjointed trauma memory, but the betrayal appraisal introduces a different interpersonal trauma theme that is not supported by the other selected items. With combat trauma, betrayal can occur, but here there are no corresponding triggers, memory content, or threat/appraisal items suggesting moral injury, friendly-fire, command betrayal, or interpersonal violation. This makes the betrayal item the main clinically incoherent element relative to the rest of the profile and formulation.

vignette:
Elena has worked at the same community bank for fifteen years, and from her station at Teller Window 3, she believes she can see danger before it arrives. It’s in the way a man shifts his weight from one foot to the other, the bulge of a wallet in a back pocket that could be something else, the flicker of an eye toward the security camera. She has to be on guard all the time, because her experience has taught her a fundamental truth: the world is a profoundly dangerous place. This conviction makes her an exemplary employee on paper—meticulous, observant, never short on her drawer. In reality, she spends her days in a state of taut, exhausting vigilance, her body thrumming with a readiness for a catastrophe that never comes. When a car backfires on the street outside, her heart hammers against her ribs and the blood drains from her face, a violent physical reaction that leaves her dizzy and breathless long after the sound has faded.

Thirty years ago, as a young army medic, she learned this lesson in the dust and chaos of a forward operating base. The memory of that day doesn't play like a film; it exists in searing, disjointed snapshots. There is the memory of shouting, then a brilliant, deafening roar that threw her against a wall of sandbags. When she tries to explain what happened next, the thread frays. She starts to describe crawling toward Sergeant Miller, but then the sequence shatters. Was the choking dust before or after she felt for his pulse? She remembers the strange, almost peaceful look on his face, and the rough, gritty texture of his canvas fatigues under her frantic hands. That texture is a ghost that follows her. Last week, when a courier dropped a coarse canvas bank bag on her counter, she flinched so violently she knocked over her pen holder. The memory is so extreme, so saturated with smoke and the scent of iron, that it’s hard for her to believe it actually happened to her. It feels like a story about someone else, a brutal film she was forced to watch.

In the years that followed, she tried to build a life far from that noise and dust. She married, raised a daughter, and found the quiet, orderly world of banking. But the vigilance never left. It became a permanent part of her, a low hum of anxiety that eventually wore down her marriage. Her ex-husband used to call her distant, saying it was like living with a ghost. He wasn’t wrong. She had come to see connection as a liability, another potential loss waiting to happen. Now, when customers she has known for years stand at her window and talk about a death in the family—a husband lost to cancer, a parent’s funeral—a cold dread seeps into her bones. She offers the scripted condolences, but inside, she is back on that dusty ground, the weight of a life slipping away under her hands.

The fallout from that day has bleached the color from her world. Nothing in her life feels meaningful anymore. Her daughter is grown and lives in another state. Her evenings are silent, spent in her small apartment where she methodically checks the locks twice before sitting in a chair that faces the door. She doesn't watch TV or read; she just sits, listening to the sounds of the building, cataloging potential threats. It was after a particularly bad day at work, when a construction crew dropped a steel beam nearby and the resulting bang sent her diving behind her counter in a full-blown panic attack, that her manager insisted she take some time off and speak to someone. Elena agreed, not because she believed it would help, but because she was terrified of losing the one piece of structure left in her life. She has come to therapy seeking not peace, which feels impossible, but a way to simply keep functioning. What she is most afraid of is that the world is exactly as dangerous as she believes it to be, and that she will never feel safe again.
